input: Given question: A 38 year old male presents with morning stiffness and pain in lower back/buttocks which improves on exercise. He has has a history of chronic back pain which also sometimes wakes him up during the night. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Spondylosis Option B: Herniates IV disk Option C: Spondylolisthesis Option D: Ankylosing Spondyilitis Option E: Quada Equina Syndrome The correct answer is Option D.
reference: A - Spondylosis - This is a condition which refers to the degenerative osteoarthritis of the joints between the spinal vertebrae/ facet joints. As it progresses the patient does have a stiff back/restricted movement. Pain is worse in the morning and evening BUT is made worse with extended activity B - Herniates IV disk - Usually occurs in the L4/L5 OR L5/S1 vertebrae. Although it usually occurs in men and aged 30-50 the pain is of sudden onset, whilst twisting or lifting heavy objects. Also the pain is usually relieved with lying down flat. C - Spondylolisthesis - Is a complication of spondylosis where there is a defect in the pars interarticularis which makes it become detached. This can then cause the vertebrae to slip out of place. Symptoms include lower back pain when standing or on activity, tenderness, stiffness and tingling radiating down legs. D - Ankylosing spondylitis - The CORRECT answer - The symptoms fit within the classifications which is chronic back pain accompanied with 3/4 of the following - morning stiffness, improvement of pain with exercise, awakening at night because of pain, alternating buttock pain. Is characterised by inflammation of the spine, fusing of the sacroiliac joints which can progress to most of the spine (bamboo spine) and maintained lumbar lordosis in flexion. ALSO usually presents in patients under 50 E - Quada Equina Syndrome - Is caused by compression of the nerves in the cauda equina. Symptoms include 1 or more of the following: bladder dysfunction (urinary retention in 50-70%), reduced sensation in perineal area, sexual dysfunction, neurological defects in the lower limb.

However, the fact that the pain improves on exercise indicates that it is most likely AS. Other diagnoses such as herniated disk and spondylolisthesis could also cause radicular pain which would not necessarily improve with exercise. Spondylosis is a bit of a catchall term for chronic back pain and does not really have any specific characteristic other than being old. Quada Equina Syndrome would likely cause more severe and constant pain which would not really be alleviated by exercise.  Source: Baku's lecture on spinal diseases. input: Given question: Nia is a 20 year old patient who has a history of anxiety and depression. She visits her GP as part of her routine medication review. She describes to the GP how after not doing as well as she had hoped in a test, she now believes that she will never get the grades she wants and will never go to uni. Based on this, she has decided not to apply for uni. What is the most likely form of thinking stratergy? Option A: Arbitrary interferences Option B: Black and white thinking Option C: Catastrophising Option D: Personalising Option E: Selective Thinking The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Arbitrary interferences - drawing negative conclusions off the back of insufficient evidenceBlack and white thinking - seeing everything in terms of success or failureCatastrophising - exaggerating a minor setback until it becomes a complete disaster Personalising - taking responsibility and blame for all unpleasant things that happenSelective thinking - focusing on negative details or events whilst ignoring positive ones

This can be challenged using the 5 whys technique. Arbitrary interferences - a person believes that their thoughts are being intercepted or controlled by someone or something. Black and white thinking - a person believes that something is either good or bad, without any shades of grey. This can be challenged using the reframing technique. Catastrophising - this is where a person assumes that the worst possible outcome will happen. This can be challenged by asking what the chances are of the worst happening, and what other outcomes could be more likely. Personalisation - a person believes that everything is their fault and that they are completely responsible for everything. This can be challenged by asking what evidence there is that they are completely responsible for everything. Selective thinking - a person only focuses on one possible outcome, and ignores all other possibilities. This can be challenged by asking what other outcomes could be possible, and what the chances of those outcomes are. input: Given question: A 27-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea, and a subsequent pregnancy test gives a positive result. She takes a lithium-based drug to treat her schizophrenia; lithium is known to have teratogenic effects such as inhibiting the formation of new blood vessels from endothelial cells in the embryo. Which process, described above, is inhibited by lithium? Option A: Angiogenesis Option B: Arborisation Option C: Haematopoiesis Option D: Somatogenesis Option E: Vasculogenesis The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Angiogenesis - Formation of new blood vessels from the sprouting of new capillaries from pre-existing vessels.Arborisation - 'Branching out' of a structure such as a nerve fibre or blood vessel. In the embryo, placental capillaries arborise to increase the blood and nutrient supply to the developing foetus.Haematopoiesis - Formation of new blood cells.Somatogenesis - The process of somite formation. Somites differentiate to specialise into different cell types depending on their location.Vasculogenesis - De novo development of blood vessels from endothelial cells differentiating in situ. Key to the provision of nutrition to the foetus. Angiogenesis and vasculogenesis may be confused with one another. Vasculogenesis comes first and occurs in utero, whereas angiogenesis occurs across one's lifetime - angiogenic disease processes include retinopathy and tumour vascularisation. In this question, vasculogenesis is correct as the stem refers to de novo formation from endothelial cells. From Dave Wilson's lecture on 'Embryology of the Cardiovascular System' in Case 8. reference: The correct answer is C. Lynch Syndrome  Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition that occurs due to mutations in MMR genes that lead to defective DNA mismatch repair leading to microsatellite instablity in tumors.  Microsatellite instability refers to the fact that microsatellites, which are naturally occurring highly repeated short DNA sequences, become shorter or longer than normal. PDF. https://elsevierelibrary.co.uk/product/kumar-clarks-clinical-medicine80515/422 )  Lynch syndrome leads to an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer. Lynch syndrome is different to the conditions in A,B,D and E because it does not tend to be associated with adenomas.  The main line of treatment is surgery- colectomy. Aspirin has been shown to be effective in reducing risk of colorectal cancer. input: Given question: Lucy, a 21 year old woman, visits her GP with a cramping pain in her stomach. The GP asks if she could be pregnant, to which Lucy responds she is '95% sure she isn't'. The GP asks Lucy to obtain a urine sample to test. Though the pregnancy test comes back as negative, the GP also tests Lucy's urine to see if there any abnormalities, and finds a high level of glucose present.  On further questioning, Lucy says that she had been feeling more fatigued recently, although had put this down to exam stress. She also said she had felt a little bit thirsty, but hadn't been concerned by this. Lucy's mum has type 2 diabetes, which she was diagnosed with 5 years ago and this had come as a shock to Lucy's mum as she had always lived what she considered to be a 'healthy lifestyle'.  After confidently ruling out that the cramping pain is not a sign of anything serious, you run a further series of tests on Lucy and diagnose her with MODY (Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young). By what pattern of inheritance is MODY passed on? Option A: Autosomal recessive Option B: X-linked recessive Option C: Autosomal dominant Option D: It is not an inherited disease Option E: X-linked dominant The correct answer is Option C.
reference: The answer is C, autosomal dominant.  The onset of MODY is typically below 25 years and it is commonly diagnosed accidentally, with the person not even being aware that they have any symptoms. It is not due to obesity, there is no ketosis and there is no beta-cell autoimmunity.  It is likely that Lucy's mum, who was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, actually has MODY and has been misdiagnosed. Lucy could have therefore inherited the condition from her mother, in an autosomal dominant pattern.

This means that a person with an autosomal dominant condition has a 50% chance of passing the condition on to each of their children.  The affected person will have two copies of the gene, one inherited from their mother and one inherited from their father. reference: After fertilisation, the zygote secretes hCG to prevent the regression of the corpus luteum so it will continue to secrete progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining of the uterus. Serotonin syndrome is an adverse drug reaction which can occur in patients on antidepressants (SSRIs) and is more likely to occur in patients who are on multiple antidepressants at once. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A 28-year old women presents to A&E after she fainted on the way to her car after work: you see she is struggling to breath and she admits to SOB and tiredness for the last few weeks. She was diagnosed Crohn's disease 8 years ago. She recently had a stomach bug, causing her to vomit several times a day. You notice a nasty abrasion on the palm of her hand where she fell, which is oozing blood and looks dirty. You do some tests... Haemoglobin: 98 g/L (115-165)Ferritin: 20 ng/mL (12-150)Folate: 4.8 ng/mL (>4)B12: 140 pg/ML (180-1000)MCV: 103 fL (80-100)  Her O2 sats on air are 93%. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment Option A: B12 injection Option B: clean and dress the wound, give a tetanus booster Option C: cross-matched blood transfusion Option D: high-flow oxygen Option E: IV iron-transfusion The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Remember basic principles: DRs ABCDE - her breathing is compromised. As her O2 sats on air are below 94% on air, oxygen is recommended. This is something simple and quick you can do to slightly relieve symptoms and stabilise while you investigate the cause! After combatting the breathing, the circulation is as issue as she is bleeding! The wound needs cleaning and dressing, and a tetatnus booster is recommended. Antibiotics may me indicated. N.B. if the bleeding excessive, and she was at risk of bleeding out, this would be addressed by the paramedics before the oxygen. Hopefully you have correctly identified that she has a B12 deficiency; this is likely caused by the stomach bug, on top of her existing Crohn's disease. The most common site of crohn's is ileocaecal junction, and B12 absorbed in the terminal ileum, hence risk of deficiency. Excessive vomitting from a stomach bug would reduce levels of stomach acid, which is needed for B12 release from food. This is causing a macrocytic anaemia (hence raised MCV).  So after the oxygen and wound dressing she should be treated with B12 injection. A blood transfusion may help with sever anaemia but wont treat the underlying cause (B12 deficiency) and would only be used if the Hb was very low. IV iron transfusion is not indicated as she does not have an Fe deficiency (ferritin normal); however if she did, IV iron may be better than oral iron as Crohn's oral Fe may not be absorbed properly.
best_explanation: This patient has anaemia secondary to B12/Folate deficiency. She is also immunocompromised (Crohn's disease). She has a wound infection which is getting into her blood (bacteraemia). She is hypoxemic. First line of treatment is oxygen. If she was in a less severe condition (e.g. mild or no oxygen requirement, no immunocompromised, no evidence of infection/sepsis) then B12 injections may be considered.  Note: iron transfusions are only given if the ferritin level is <15 and the patient is symptomatic (tired, SOB etc.)  Folate/B12/iron deficiency anaemia can be caused by: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune, causing immune destruction of intrinsic factor)Crohn's disease (B12/folate malabsorption)Ulcerative colitis (folate malabsorption)Chronic alcohol consumptionDrug/chemical exposure (methotrexate, anti-convulsants, anti-psychotics)  The most common cause of macrocytic (high MCV) anaemia is B12/folate deficiency. The most common cause of microcytic (low MCV) anaemia is iron-deficiency anaemia.  http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2972015/table/T1/ for more info on anaemia types.

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Dan presents to the GP with back pain. On examination, he has a loss of vibration sensation and proprioception. His MRC is grade 5 in all areas. Pain and temperature sensation are normal. What is the most likely pathology underlying these symptoms? Option A: A tumour of the laminae of some of his vertebrae Option B: Nerve root compression Option C: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery Option D: Penetrating spinal injury Option E: Reduced blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord The correct answer is Option A.
reference: The symptoms suggest that this patient has posterior cord syndrome. This is because vibration sensation and proprioception are affected and these run in the dorsal column at the posterior of the spinal cord. Motor function and pain / temperature sensation are fins so the anterior of the spinal cord isn't affected. Posterior cord syndrome is usually caused by something compressing the posterior spinal artery. For example a tumour in the posterior of the vertebral bodies could do this. A (spinal tumour) - CORRECTB (nerve root compression) - this is radiculopathy. Symptoms are lower motor neurone symptoms (weakness, severe and focal atrophy, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, may be fasciculations) as the nerve root contains LMNsC (anterior spinal artery occlusion) - this causes anterior cord syndrome. The corticospinal tract is damaged so there is loss of motor function. The spinothalamic tract is damaged so there is loss of pain, temperature and fine touch sensation. The dorsal column remains in tact so vibration sensation and proprioception are preservedD (penetrating spinal injury) - can cause Brown-Sequard syndrome if only one side of the spinal cord is injured. The corticospinal tract is damaged so there is ipsilateral loss of motor function as it has already decussated in the medulla. The spinothalamic tract is damaged so there is contralateral loss of pain, temperature and fine touch sensation as it has not yet decussated. The dorsal column is damaged so there is ipsilateral loss of vibration sensation and proprioception as it has already decussated in the medullaE (reduced blood supply centrally) - can cause central cord syndrome. Blood supply of the spinal cord is peripheral to central so the centre is more vulnerable. All the tracts are damaged so there is loss of motor function and sensation. The tracts are laminated so that the cervical parts are towards the centre, followed by the thoracic and lumbar parts and finally the sacral parts towards the periphery. Because of this, the upper limbs (which are controlled by more central parts of the spinal cord) will be affected more than the lower limbs and recovery will be from the lower limbs upwards This was covered in the case 14 tutorial ‘CORD SYNDROMES’.
best_explanation: A tumour of the laminae of some of his vertebrae is most likely as this would compress the posterior aspect of the spinal cord resulting in loss of vibration sensation and proprioception (and probably motor function as well given the grade 5 MRC) Nerve root compression would result in loss of nerve supply to the posterior aspect of the spinal cord resulting in loss of vibration sensation and proprioception but pain and temperature sensation would be preserved as would the motor function given the grade 5 MRC Pain and temperature sensation would be lost in both of these conditions as would motor function given the grade 5 MRC Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery would result in loss of blood supply to the anterior aspect of the spinal cord resulting in loss of pain and temperature sensation as well as vibration sensation and proprioception given the grade 5 MRC A penetrating spinal injury would result in loss of blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord resulting in loss of pain and temperature sensation as well as vibration sensation and proprioception Reduced blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord would result in loss of pain and temperature sensation as well as vibration sensation and proprioception  For those who like pictures: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537101/table/A5176567/ This was covered in the case 12 lecture ‘NEUROLOGICAL AND RADIOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES’. The lecture also covers epidural spinal tumours in greater detail. input: Given question: An elderly patient with heart failure is prescribed DIGOXIN. What is the mechanism of action of this drug? Option D: Digoxin blocks the NCX in the cardiomyocyte which flips the movement of ions across the Na+/K+ ATPase causing an increase in intracellular calcium. Option E: Digoxin blocks the NCX in the cardiomyocyte which flips the movement of ions across the Na+/K+ ATPase causing an increase in intracellular sodium. The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Digoxin acts as a positive inotrope in treating congestive heart failure. Digoxin acts by binding to the ATPase which consequently results in the movement of ions across the NCX flipping, so that sodium moves out and calcium moves in. This increases the force of contraction. It is often prescribed to elderly sedentary patients with heart failure, but is not usually a 1st line therapy. input: Given question: Velma the Virus has a plan. Using her cunning, skills and womanly good looks, she intends to infiltrate the defences of the hairy medical student she has just entered, and then cause havoc and woe. But first, she must evade the student's sentinel cells, lest they present her antigens to their commanders. Wait! What's that?  Which of these is NOT a sentinel cell? reference: Sentinel cells are the body's "first line of defense". They are fixed WBCs which detect and bind to pathogens. Some release interferons in response.  Macrophages phagocytose invading organisms, and release cytokines in response.Microglial cells perform the same role as macrophages, within the CNS.Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells which travel to the lymph nodes once they have processed an antigen. Langerhans cells are dendritic cells found within the skin and mucosa, and are not to be confused with the Islets of Langerhans. Natural killer cells are not sentinel cells. They detect cells which have been infected, and destroy them.

Langerhans cells are dendritic cells found in the skin.  All of these cells are capable of recognising pathogens and presenting antigens to the immune system.  Natural killer cells recognise and attack pathogens in a non-specific manner, without prior activation of the immune system. These include increased Ca2+ movement into the cell (Via L-type Ca2+ channels), causing increased Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Which receptor on the SR is stimulated to cause this CICR (Calcium induced calcium release)?What effect will this have on the cardiac cycle? Option A: HCN4 channels Increased Chronotropy Option B: Ryanodine receptorsIncreased Inotropy and accelerated Lucitropy Option C: HCN4 channels Increased Inotropy Option D: Ryanodine receptors Decreased Inotropy and accelerated Lucitropy Option E: HCN4 receptors Increased Lucitropy The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart via beta adrenergic receptors activates the PKA signalling cascade, this causes phosphorylation of L-type Ca2+ channels,  increasing Ca2+ movement into the cellThis Ca2+ binds to Ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (an intracellular store of Ca2+)This causes release of Ca2+ from the SR (CICR). This surge in Ca2+ in the myocyte causes increased contractility of the cell (increased inotropy)The PKA cascade also phosphorylates phospholamban, speeding up SR Ca2+ reuptake, this increased reuptake rapidly reduces Ca2+ in the cell after release, causing accelerated relaxation (Lucitropy) Sources T.J Allen lecture 'Regulation of excitation & contraction in the heart'Khan academy medicine 'Increasing ventricular contractility - inotropic effect' (the series on autonomic regulation of the heart is nice and simple, makes the TJ lecture a lot easier!)https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/nerve-regulation-of-the-heart/v/increasing-ventricular-contractility-inotropic-effectThe second paragraph of this article explains the Lucitropy bit wellhttp://www.sci.utah.edu/~macleod/bioen/be6003/notes/1.Sympathetic-Activation.pdf Learning objectivesDescribe, compare and contrast chronotropic and inotropic regulation in the heartDescribe the regulation of lusitropy in cardiomyocytes
best_explanation: Beta adrenergic receptors are Gs protein coupled receptors which activate adenylyl cyclase, increasing levels of cAMP.This causes an increase in activity of the protein kinase A (PKA) which increases the activity of the SR Ca2+ pump (PMCA).This increases the amount of Ca2+ reuptaken into the SR, so less Ca2+ is released into the myocyte.Less Ca2+ release means less contraction, meaning the myocyte relaxes for longer, therefore increasing R-R interval and decelerating chronotropy.Increased Ca2+ reuptake means more Ca2+ is available for release later, meaning that more Ca2+ is released into the myocyte on subsequent contractions, meaning more inotropy.This is because the SR Ca2+ pump is sensitive to cAMP, therefore when cAMP increases, PMCA increases Ca2+ reuptake, meaning more Ca2+ is available for release later.Ryanodine receptors are activated by calcium, and cause the sudden release of Ca2+ from the SR, causing a rapid increase in intracellular Ca2+ which causes a larger contraction, therefore accelerating lucitropy.Due to the increase in Ca2+ reuptake, less Ca2+ is released into the myocyte, meaning less inotropy.The HCN4 channels are Na+ channels which are activated by Ca2+.When more Ca2+ is released into the myocyte, the HCN4 channels open more, causing an increased chronotropy.The HCN4 channels are not directly affected by beta adrenergic receptors.Therefore the correct answer is B. (Although E would also be correct, as increased Ca2+ reuptake will increase the amount of Ca2+ available for lucitropy, meaning more rapid deceleration of lucitropy.) (TJ Allen lecture, case 13)

input: Given question: After a busy day at work, Mike cleans his teeth and gets into bed. After 10 minutes he is starting to sleep. As he drifts off he has a strange hallucination of a figure in his room. What waves would be seen on an EEG at this time? Option A: alpha and beta Option B: alpha and theta Option C: theta waves interrupted by sleep spindles Option D: delta waves Option E: high frequency waves resembling beta waves The correct answer is Option B.
reference: We would expect Mike to be in NREM sleep stage 1  When a patient is awake with eyes open the EEG will show mainly beta waves. When the patient goes to bed and closes their eyes alpha waves will be seen.• Sleep stage 1 produces alpha and theta waves which are low frequency and high amplitude. May experience hallucinations and hypnic jerks which are muscle twitches• During REM sleep high frequency waves that mostly resemble beta waves are seen. The body is paralysed apart from the eyes and swallowing. This is when dreams happen.• Sleep stage 2 is dominated by theta waves, interrupted by sleep spindles which are bursts or rapid activity. K complexes can also be seen in this stage which are spikes of activity. Sleep talking and teeth grinding happen in this stage• NREM stage N3- deep sleep- is associated with long delta waves. These have a large amplitude and low-frequency. This is where sleep talking, night terrors and bed wetting can occur.

You notice the patient has good flexion of the lumbar spine but extension is limited. The straight leg raise test is negative.   What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Peripheral arterial disease Option B: Spinal stenosis Option C: Prolapsed IV disc Option D: Chronic mechanical back pain Option E: Metastatic spinal cord compression The correct answer is Option B.
reference: A - this is worth considering as the patient complains of claudication (pain in the leg on activity). However, vascular claudication is usually relieved by standing up opposed to sitting down. You may also observe trophic changes to the skin during examination in vascular disease.  B - this is the correct answer. Firstly the patient is over 50 which is an important risk factor for spinal stenosis. Moreover there is noticeable pain on extension. For example the patient says the pain is worst walking down hills but relieved by sittting. Extension of the lumbar spine narrows the spinal canal and can increase pressure on nervous tissue. This explains the patient’s neurogenic claudication. C - although the patient complained of tingling in both legs the straight leg raise is negative. Moreover patients with prolapsed IV disc usually find it uncomfortable to sit. D - the history does not fit with this diagnosis. Moreover metastatic cord compression is a medical emergency and the patient will often present acutely with ‘hard’ neurological signs such as loss of bowel control.

input: Given question: Monica presents to her GP with a high fever, muscle weakness and a sore mouth, with bleeding gums. On examination she is hypotensive and tachycardic. Upon reviewing Monica's drug history the GP thinks she might be experiencing agranulocytosis. What is the most likely drug he is attributing to the manifestation of this condition? Option A: Sertraline Option B: Atorvostatin Option C: Bisoprolol Option D: Clozapine Option E: Risperidone The correct answer is Option D.
reference: The answer is D, clozapine, a 2nd generation anti-psychotic. Due to the risk of these side effects it is not given first line, only for treatment resistant patients. Agranulocytosis is when there is dangerously low white blood cells causing neutropenia. It is thought that clozapine is able to produce an ion that binds to neutrophils, hence inducing this condition.
best_explanation: The correct answer is D: clozapine.  This is a second generation antipsychotic and it's most likely to cause agranulocytosis because it has a high affinity for D2 receptors and D4 receptors.  Sertraline, atorvostatin and bisoprolol do not cause agranulocytosis. Risperidone is an atypical antipsychotic and can also cause agranulocytosis. input: Given question: A patient walks into your surgery looking fairly jaundiced. On approach, you notice that he also he reeks of alcohol and he mentions to you that he just lost his job (which turns out to be 3 months previously) so decided to go on a bender since then. Clearly he has alcohol dependency issues that seem to have an effect on his bile secretion. To figure out how much alcohol (in units) he is drinking to cause such damage, you ask him what he has a day. He says, (as expected), 'not much doctor, just 2 bottles of vodka and 12 cans of cider. But it's not bad doc, I start off with the ciders and then have the vodka in between, like a water break... but with vodka...'.Trying not to look shocked or judgemental, you tell him the total number of units he's consuming. What is the figure you told him? Volume of vodka per bottle 1L, percentage of alcohol by volume (ABV) 40%Volume of cider per can 500ml, percentage ABV 7.5% Option A: 120 units Option B: 45 units Option C: 67.5 units Option D: 125 units Option E: 80 units The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Formula: [(Total of volume in a drink in (ml) X Alcohol by volume (%))/1000] So for vodka: (2 x 1000) x (40) /1000 = 80 units Cider: (12 x 500) x (7.5) /1000 = 45 units Total = 125 units *ABV is the measure of a drink's strength. It's the amount of pure alcohol expressed as a percentage of the total volume of liquid in a drink.
